d1-1.ev: Truscott's US 3rd Infantry Division comes ashore at dawn on the beaches either side of Licata.

q.t: Which division landed at Licata?
q.x: Major General Lucian Truscott's US 3rd Infantry Division landed either side of Licata and took the town on the first day.

d1-1.rem: Licata was the westernmost landing, and its small harbour quickly became a supply port for Seventh Army.
d1-1.st: At dawn on 10 July 1943 Major General Lucian Truscott's US 3rd Infantry Division came ashore on the beaches either side of Licata, the westernmost of the Allied landings. The division took the town and its small harbour on the first day, and the port quickly became a supply base for Seventh Army. A stop here sets the scale of an invasion front some 150 kilometres long. Today the harbour mole gives a view of the landing beaches to east and west.

d1-2.ev: The Rangers attack Gela directly while the 1st Infantry Division lands on the beaches to the east.

q.t: What saved the American beachhead at Gela over the next two days?
o: Naval gunfire and artillery landed on the beach
q.x: Italian and German tanks came close to throwing the Americans back into the sea; only naval gunfire and artillery landed on the beach saved the beachhead.

d1-2.rem: Gela was the heart of the American landings, and for two days the beachhead nearly failed here.
d1-2.st: Gela was the heart of the American landings on 10 July 1943. The Rangers attacked the town directly, clearing the old town on its ridge street by street, while the 1st Infantry Division landed on the beaches to the east. Over the next two days Italian and German tanks came close to throwing the Americans back into the sea. Only naval gunfire and artillery landed on the beach saved the beachhead. Today a modern pier stands on the site of the one blown in 1943, with the long beaches stretching away to the east.

d1-3.ev: Paratroopers and 1st Division infantry hold the crossroads pillboxes as German armour thrusts towards the beaches.

q.t: Who led the small group of paratroopers that took the pillboxes here?
q.x: A small group of 505th paratroopers under Captain Edwin Sayre took the complex of Italian pillboxes at Piano Lupo.

d1-3.rem: Piano Lupo was a paratroop objective for the night of 9–10 July, held against German tanks on 11 July.
d1-3.st: Piano Lupo was the road junction the 505th paratroopers were meant to seize on the night of 9–10 July 1943. A small group under Captain Edwin Sayre took the complex of Italian pillboxes here. Joined by infantry of the 1st Division, they held the crossroads against the German armoured thrust of 11 July, which was stopped on the Gela plain to the south. Today some Italian pillboxes survive on the slope of the Niscemi road, on private farmland, and can be seen from the roadside.

d1-4.ev: Paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne fight near the Acate river, and Gavin stops the Tigers on Biazza Ridge.
d1-4.rem: The main American memorial to the Sicily campaign names paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne killed nearby.
d1-4.st: Beside the SS115, where it crosses the Acate or Dirillo river, stands the main American memorial to the Sicily campaign. It lists paratroopers of the 82nd Airborne Division who were killed in the fighting nearby. About three kilometres to the east lies Biazza Ridge, where Colonel James Gavin stopped the German Tiger tanks. A ceremony is held here every July to remember them. Today the memorial tablet stands beside the restored Italian bunkers of the Ponte Dirillo strongpoint, looking east towards the ridge.

d1-5.ev: The 1st Canadian Infantry Division comes ashore, taking Canada's first steps on Italian soil.

q.t: What grounded some landing craft off Bark West beach?
q.x: The shallow water and offshore sandbars that grounded some landing craft are still there on this almost unchanged beach.

d1-5.rem: Canada's part in the Italian campaign began on this almost unchanged beach.
d1-5.st: On 10 July 1943 the 1st Canadian Infantry Division came ashore here, beginning Canada's part in the Italian campaign. Royal Marine Commandos landed on the western sector, and the first Canadian steps on Italian soil were taken on this sand. The beach is almost unchanged since then: low dunes, shallow water and the offshore sandbars that grounded some of the landing craft. Today a Canadian flag marks the spot, and the Roger and Sugar sectors of the landing beach stretch away to the west.

d1-6.ev: Canadians, the 51st Highland Division and other Eighth Army units land on the beaches south and east of Pachino.

q.t: Which Allied army landed on the beaches around Pachino?
q.x: The monument recalls the landings by the Canadians, the 51st Highland Division and other units of Eighth Army.

d1-6.rem: Pachino's monument remembers Eighth Army's landings on the beaches south and east of the town.
d1-6.st: On 10 July 1943 the beaches south and east of Pachino were among the landing places of Eighth Army. The Canadians, the 51st Highland Division and other units came ashore here, at the south-eastern corner of Sicily. A modern monument in front of the town hall recalls those landings and the men who made them. Today it stands in the town square, with its inscription, and makes a quick stop and a place for coffee on the drive north to Syracuse.

d1-7.ev: Commonwealth soldiers killed in the landings and the first days ashore, many of them glider-borne men, are laid to rest.
d1-7.rem: About 1,060 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, many of them glider-borne men of Operation Ladbroke.
d1-7.st: About 1,060 Commonwealth soldiers are buried at Syracuse, most of them killed in the landings of July 1943 and the first days ashore. Among them are many glider-borne men of Operation Ladbroke. British, Indian, South African, Canadian and other graves show how multinational Eighth Army was, and how young most of the dead were. Today the cemetery is a quiet place, with the Cross of Sacrifice, the headstones of the glider pilots and airlanding soldiers, and the rows of Indian graves.

d1-8.ev: The last fifteen unwounded glider men holding the bridge surrender, less than an hour before relief arrives.

q.t: What happened less than an hour after the last defenders surrendered?
o: The Germans blew up the bridge
The relief force arrived and retook it intact
A second wave of gliders landed
q.x: The last fifteen unwounded defenders surrendered at 15:30, less than an hour before the relief force arrived and retook the bridge intact.

d1-8.rem: A few dozen men held the bridge for most of 10 July; it was retaken intact within the hour.
d1-8.st: Ponte Grande, just south of Syracuse, was the objective of the first large British glider operation of the war. A few dozen men held the bridge for most of 10 July 1943. At 15:30 the last fifteen unwounded defenders surrendered, less than an hour before the relief force arrived and retook it intact. The prize it protected, the city of Syracuse, lay just beyond. Today the bridge still crosses the Anapo at the southern edge of the city, among the canal ditches where the defenders fought.

d2-1.ev: British and German paratroopers fight for the Simeto bridge that opens the road to Catania.

q.t: Who fought whom at Primosole Bridge?
q.x: The battle set British Red Devils against German Fallschirmjäger in one of the first clashes between rival paratroops.

d2-1.rem: Losing Primosole cost Montgomery three weeks on the Catania plain beyond.
d2-1.st: From 13 to 16 July 1943 British and German paratroopers fought for this bridge over the Simeto river. Holding it meant opening the road to Catania; losing it cost Montgomery three weeks on the plain beyond. The battle set the British Red Devils against the German Fallschirmjäger in one of the first clashes between rival paratroops. Today the bridge carries the busy SS114, with memorials beside the road and the river banks where the paratroops dug in.

d2-2.ev: The fallen of Primosole and the Catania plain, most of 1st Parachute Brigade's dead among them, are buried.
d2-2.rem: About 2,135 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, including most of the fallen paratroopers of 1st Parachute Brigade.
d2-2.st: About 2,135 Commonwealth soldiers are buried at Catania, many of them killed at Primosole and in the fighting for the Catania plain in the summer of 1943. The cemetery holds most of the fallen paratroopers of 1st Parachute Brigade, as well as Highlanders and Durham men who fought for the Gerbini airfields and the Simeto crossings. Etna rises above the plain that Eighth Army could not cross for three weeks. Today the cemetery lies west of Catania airport, a quiet place among the paratroopers' and Durham Light Infantry graves.

d2-3.ev: Soldiers of both sides and Sicilian civilians live through the invasion and campaign of summer 1943.

q.t: Whose war photographs fill a large display in the museum?
q.x: The museum has a large display of Phil Stern's war photographs; Capa's pictures hang in Troina.

d2-3.rem: Sicily's main 1943 museum tells the campaign from Allied, Axis and civilian points of view.
d2-3.st: The Allied invasion of July 1943 turned Sicily into a battlefield, for soldiers of both sides and for the people who lived there. This museum, the island's main museum of the campaign, tells that story from Allied, Axis and civilian points of view. It fills the converted sulphur works of Le Ciminiere with uniforms, weapons and reconstructed scenes, including an air-raid shelter and a Sicilian village square. Today its large display of Phil Stern's war photographs is one of the highlights of a visit.

d2-4.ev: German soldiers killed in Sicily, most of them very young, are gathered at the foot of Etna.
d2-4.rem: 4,561 German dead lie here, 451 of them unidentified, among them the Olympic long jumper Luz Long.
d2-4.st: The German war cemetery for Sicily holds 4,561 dead, 451 of them unidentified, in a walled vault building at the foot of Etna. Most of those who lie here were very young. Among them is Luz Long, the long jumper who befriended Jesse Owens at the 1936 Olympics. The cemetery is a reminder that the campaign of 1943 took young lives on both sides. Today visitors pass through five raised courtyards, with the comrades' grave in the first and the bronze figure of a dying youth.

d2-5.ev: The 38th (Irish) Brigade storms the cliff-top town against German paratroopers.

q.t: Which brigade stormed Centuripe?
q.x: The 38th (Irish) Brigade of the British 78th Division stormed Centuripe on 2–3 August against German paratroopers.

d2-5.rem: Centuripe's fall cracked the German Etna line and helped decide the evacuation of the island.
d2-5.st: On 2–3 August 1943 the 38th (Irish) Brigade of the British 78th Division stormed this cliff-top town, held by German paratroopers. Its fall cracked the German Etna line and helped decide Kesselring and Hube to plan the evacuation of Sicily. Montgomery is reported to have said he doubted any other division in his army could have done it. Today the town gives wide views over the Simeto and Salso valleys to Etna and Adrano, above the slopes the Irish battalions climbed.

d2-6.ev: The Canadian dead of Sicily are gathered on a hilltop looking across to Agira and Etna.
d2-6.rem: 490 Canadians killed in Sicily lie here, in the island's only Canadian war cemetery.
d2-6.st: Agira holds Sicily's only Canadian war cemetery, where the Canadian dead of the 1943 campaign were gathered. 490 Canadians killed on the island lie on a hilltop above Lake Pozzillo, looking across to Agira and Etna. The town itself saw the Canadians' hardest fighting of the campaign in late July. The cemetery has been a place of pilgrimage for Canadians since 1943, and walkers who retrace the division's route end here. Today the terraced rows and a visitors' book full of Canadian messages keep that bond.

d2-7.ev: The Americans fight their hardest battle in Sicily for the ridge-top town of Troina.

q.t: Whose photographs are shown in the Troina museum?
q.x: The museum in the Palazzo Pretura shows 62 prints by Robert Capa, who photographed the fighting and the ruined town.

d2-7.rem: Troina was the hardest American battle in Sicily, recorded by Robert Capa's camera.
d2-7.st: Between 31 July and 6 August 1943 Troina was the scene of the hardest American battle in Sicily, fought by the US 1st Infantry Division. Robert Capa photographed the fighting and the ruined town, and his pictures record soldiers and civilians alike. The museum in the Palazzo Pretura now shows 62 of his prints. From the upper town, the hills the 1st Division attacked spread out to the west and south. Today the photographs and the views together make the battle easy to picture.

d3-1.ev: The German 29th Panzergrenadier Division holds the US 3rd Division on the ridge above the Furiano.

q.t: What finally broke the German hold on San Fratello ridge?
o: A frontal attack across the Furiano
Taking Hill 673 and a landing behind the line
q.x: Frontal attacks failed with heavy loss until the Americans took Hill 673 and landed behind the line at Sant'Agata.

d3-1.rem: Frontal attacks failed here; it took Hill 673 and a landing behind the line to break the ridge.
d3-1.st: From 3 to 8 August 1943 the German 29th Panzergrenadier Division held the US 3rd Division on this ridge above the Furiano river. American frontal attacks failed with heavy loss. The line was broken only when the Americans took Hill 673 and landed troops behind it at Sant'Agata, on the coast. The ridge shows how a single strong position could stall an advance along the north coast. Today the town still sits on the ridge the Germans held, below flat-topped Monte San Fratello.

d3-2.ev: Bernard's 2nd Battalion, 30th Infantry, lands behind the San Fratello line in Patton's first end run.

q.t: What did the landing force find when it came ashore?
o: A German division waiting on the beach
Most of the Germans had already pulled back
q.x: The landing achieved surprise, but most of the Germans had already pulled back from the San Fratello line.

d3-2.rem: Patton's first end run achieved surprise, but most of the Germans had already gone.
d3-2.st: At 03:15 on 8 August 1943 Patton's first amphibious end run put Bernard's 2nd Battalion, 30th Infantry, ashore on this beach. The aim was to land behind the German line at San Fratello and cut the coast road. The landing achieved surprise, but most of the Germans had already pulled back. Patton ordered a second landing, at Brolo, three days later. Today the public beach west of the Rosmarino river mouth and the coast road beside it show where the landing force came in.

d3-3.ev: Bernard's battalion lands at Brolo and holds Monte Cipolla against the 29th Panzergrenadier Division.

q.t: How many men did Bernard's battalion lose at Brolo?
q.x: The battalion held Monte Cipolla for a day and lost 177 men before the rest of the 3rd Division relieved it.

d3-3.rem: At Brolo one battalion held Monte Cipolla for a day, losing 177 men before relief arrived.
d3-3.st: On 11 August 1943 Patton tried a second end run. Bernard's battalion landed at Brolo and seized Monte Cipolla, the hill above the coast road. For a day it held out against the 29th Panzergrenadier Division, losing 177 men, before the rest of the 3rd Division broke through the Naso ridge to relieve it. The landing showed the cost of going round the enemy by sea. Today the hill between the Naso and Brolo rivers is farmland, best seen from the coast road and the seafront.

d3-4.ev: Patton enters Messina, hours after the last German boats have left across the Strait.
d3-4.rem: The shrine holds some 1,288 Italian soldiers of the Second World War and 110 of the First.
d3-4.st: Messina's military shrine holds the remains of some 1,288 Italian soldiers of the Second World War and 110 of the First. Below it lies the city Patton entered on 17 August 1943, at the end of the Sicilian campaign. Across the water is the Strait over which the Axis forces escaped to the mainland. The terrace gives the best view of both. Today a great bell, cast from captured First World War guns, rings here at sunset over the crypt and the harbour.

d3-5.ev: Night after night German ferries carry troops across the narrow Strait under a screen of flak.

q.t: Roughly how wide is the Strait at Capo Peloro?
q.x: Capo Peloro is the narrowest point of the Strait, about three kilometres across.

d3-5.rem: At its narrowest the Strait is about three kilometres wide, and flak kept Allied aircraft at bay.
d3-5.st: Capo Peloro marks the narrowest point of the Strait of Messina, about three kilometres across. In August 1943 the German ferry routes ran from the beaches between here and Messina, and flak batteries around the Strait kept Allied aircraft at bay. Short crossings and strong air defence explain why the Axis escape from Sicily succeeded. Today the lighthouse point faces the Calabrian shore; the tall pylon nearby is a relic of a 1950s power line, not the war.

d4-1.ev: Eighth Army lands almost unopposed north of Reggio, returning to the European mainland.

q.t: How strongly was the Baytown landing opposed?
o: It met a German panzer division
It was driven back into the sea
q.x: The landing of 3 September 1943 was almost unopposed, a strange beginning for a twenty-month campaign.

d4-1.rem: On 3 September 1943 Eighth Army returned to the European mainland here, almost unopposed.
d4-1.st: On 3 September 1943 Eighth Army crossed from Sicily and landed on this stretch of shore north of Reggio. It was the first Allied landing on the Italian peninsula and marked the army's return to the European mainland. The landing was almost unopposed, a strange beginning for a campaign that would last another twenty months. Today the shore lies right beside the ferry port, and from the waterline Sicily is only a few kilometres away across the strait.

d4-2.ev: The 36th Texas Division comes ashore straight into fire from the 16th Panzer Division.

q.t: Who won the Medal of Honor near here on the morning of the landing?
q.x: Sergeant James Logan won the Medal of Honor near here that morning, knocking out German machine-gun posts.

d4-2.rem: The 36th Texas Division landed here straight into fire from the 16th Panzer Division.
d4-2.st: At 03:30 on 9 September 1943 the 36th Texas Division came ashore on this beach, straight into fire from the 16th Panzer Division. That morning Sergeant James Logan won the Medal of Honor near here, knocking out German machine-gun posts. The landing was the American part of the Allied assault at Salerno, and the memorial by the shore is the best place to understand it. Today the beach runs towards the Torre di Paestum, with the flat plain, the temples and Monte Soprano inland.

d4-3.ev: Both sides treat the Greek temples as off limits, while Allied medics set up aid stations nearby.

q.t: How did both sides treat the temples in 1943?
q.x: The temples were on the edge of the beachhead, and both sides treated them as off limits.

d4-3.rem: Both sides treated the 2,500-year-old temples as off limits, while shells landed around them.
d4-3.st: In September 1943 the three great Greek temples of Paestum stood on the edge of the 36th Division's beachhead. Both sides treated them as off limits, and Allied medics set up aid stations nearby. Walking among 2,500-year-old columns where shells were landing in 1943 is one of the most striking contrasts of the whole trip. The landing beaches lie only a kilometre to the west. Today the Temple of Neptune, the Basilica and the museum's painted Tomb of the Diver are open to visitors.

d4-4.ev: The hilltop village changes hands three times in a week as the 36th Division fights for it.

q.t: Why did the 36th Division fight so hard for Altavilla?
o: From here German observers could see every beach and road
It held the division's supply dump
It controlled the bridge over the Sele
q.x: From the village German observers could see every beach and road on the plain.

d4-4.rem: From Altavilla German observers could see every beach and road on the plain below.
d4-4.st: Altavilla Silentina and Hill 424 behind it dominated the American sector at Salerno in September 1943. From here German observers could see every beach and road on the plain below. That is why the 36th Division fought so hard for the village, which changed hands three times in a week, and why it was shelled from sea and land. Today a viewpoint in the old centre looks west over the Sele plain to the sea and the landing beaches, the view the German observers had.

d4-5.ev: German armour drives down the corridor towards the beaches, threatening to split the beachhead in two.

q.t: What stopped the German attack near the Calore?
q.x: American field artillery stopped the German armour near the Calore.

d4-5.rem: On 13 September the beachhead came close to being split; American field artillery stopped the attack.
d4-5.st: On the afternoon of 13 September 1943 German armour drove down this corridor between the Sele and Calore rivers towards the beaches. The Allied beachhead came close to being split in two. American field artillery stopped the attack near the Calore. Little marks the spot, but the ground itself explains the danger. Today, from a farm road near the Calore bridge, the corridor stretches flat and open towards Persano and Altavilla.

d4-6.ev: Men of British X Corps who fought between the Sele and Salerno are laid to rest near Battipaglia.
d4-6.rem: 1,851 men lie here, 109 of them unidentified, most of them of British X Corps.
d4-6.st: The Commonwealth war cemetery for the Salerno landings of September 1943 holds 1,851 graves, 109 of them unidentified. Most are men of the British X Corps, who fought between the Sele and Salerno. The cemetery lies close to the old Montecorvino airfield and the Battipaglia battlefield. The American dead of Salerno were later moved to the US cemetery at Nettuno. Today the rows carry the regimental badges of X Corps, and a register box by the entrance lists the burials.

d4-7.ev: Salerno serves as seat of the Italian government, months after the Allied landings on its beaches.

q.t: What was Salerno from February to July 1944?
q.x: The museum tells the story of Salerno's months as seat of the Italian government, February to July 1944.

d4-7.rem: For a few months in 1944 Salerno was the seat of the Italian government.
d4-7.st: After the landings of September 1943, Salerno became the seat of the Italian government from February to July 1944. This volunteer-run museum of about 200 objects covers both the landings and those months as capital. Outside stand a Sherman tank, a jeep and a sealed railway wagon of the kind used to deport Italian Jews. The wagon is a reminder that the war in Italy was also a racial persecution. Today visits are by reservation, and uniforms and weapons of all three armies fill the rooms.

d5-1.ev: Neapolitans rise against the German occupiers, the first large Italian city to do so.

q.t: Who was Gennaro Capuozzo?
o: A street boy killed in the uprising
A British officer who entered the city
q.x: The monument honours all who fought, from soldiers to street boys like Gennaro Capuozzo, killed aged 11 or 12.

d5-1.rem: Naples was the first large Italian city to rise against the German occupiers, in the Four Days of September 1943.
d5-1.st: From 27 to 30 September 1943 the people of Naples rose against the German occupiers, the first large Italian city to do so. The Four Days drew in everyone from soldiers to street boys like Gennaro Capuozzo, killed aged 11 or 12; sources differ. This monument on the seafront at Mergellina honours all who fought. To the east lies the port the Germans wrecked. Today four carved panels tell the story, with the bay of Naples spread out beyond them.

d5-2.ev: Thousands of Neapolitans shelter in a royal tunnel and old cisterns as Allied bombers strike the city.

q.t: About how many Allied raids hit Naples between 1940 and 1944?
q.x: Naples suffered about 200 Allied raids between 1940 and 1944, making it one of the most heavily bombed cities in Italy.

d5-2.rem: Naples was one of Italy's most bombed cities; thousands sheltered in this 19th-century royal tunnel.
d5-2.st: Naples was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Italy, with about 200 Allied raids between 1940 and 1944 and civilian deaths estimated at 20,000 to 25,000. This 19th-century royal tunnel and its old cisterns became a shelter for thousands of people. Their graffiti and beds remain, along with wrecked cars left here after the war, and make the civilian experience very real. Today the shelter can be seen only on a guided tour through its rooms and past the dumped vehicles.

d5-3.ev: Men who die in the Allied hospitals of liberated Naples are buried at the edge of the city.
d5-3.rem: 1,202 Commonwealth soldiers lie here, many of them men who died in the city's Allied hospitals.
d5-3.st: Naples War Cemetery holds 1,202 Commonwealth burials of the Second World War. Many are men who died in the three general hospitals set up in the city after its liberation in October 1943. Others are soldiers moved in from small burial grounds nearby. The variety of regiments and nations reflects the whole Allied base in Naples. Today the cemetery at Miano is a quiet counterpoint to the chaos of the city centre.

d5-4.ev: German envoys sign the surrender of German and Italian Fascist forces in Italy.

q.t: When did the surrender signed here take effect?
q.x: The surrender was signed at Caserta on 29 April 1945 and took effect on 2 May.

d5-4.rem: The campaign you are following ended here, with the surrender signed on 29 April 1945.
d5-4.st: In the autumn of 1943 the vast Bourbon palace of Caserta became an Allied headquarters, first for the US Fifth Army and later for Allied Force Headquarters. Here, on 29 April 1945, German envoys signed the surrender of German and Italian Fascist forces in Italy. It took effect on 2 May, ending the campaign. Offices, map rooms and soldiers' rest camps once filled the palace and its grounds. Today the royal apartments, the grand staircase and the long park with its cascade are open to visitors.

d5-5.ev: Soldiers killed in the Volturno fighting are buried, later joined by men who die in Caserta's hospitals.
d5-5.rem: 768 Commonwealth men lie here: hospital patients, prisoners of war and soldiers of the Volturno fighting.
d5-5.st: A walled section of Caserta's town cemetery holds 768 Commonwealth burials. Some are men who died in the 2nd General Hospital, which worked here from December 1943 to September 1945. Others are prisoners of war who died in the prisoner-of-war hospital at Caserta, and soldiers killed in the Volturno fighting of October 1943, whose dates appear on many headstones. Today it is a small, peaceful plot inside the town cemetery, a short drive from the palace.

d5-6.ev: Fifth Army attacks across the flooded Volturno, the first great river obstacle north of Naples.

q.t: Which two divisions made their attempts between Capua and Triflisco?
q.x: Between Capua and the Triflisco gap the US 3rd and British 56th Divisions made their attempts to cross.

d5-6.rem: The steep banks of the flooded Volturno show why Fifth Army's first great river crossing was so hard.
d5-6.st: On the night of 12–13 October 1943 Fifth Army attacked across the flooded Volturno, the first great river obstacle north of Naples. Here, between Capua and the Triflisco gap, the US 3rd and British 56th Divisions made their attempts. The steep banks explain why the crossing was so hard, and the Germans held the ridges to the north. Today a roadside stop by the river at Capua or near Triflisco shows the obstacle, and Capua's historic centre is worth a short walk.

d5-7.ev: Italian soldiers of the co-belligerent army fight their first battle beside the Allies on Monte Lungo.
d5-7.rem: 974 Italian soldiers rest here, most from the army that fought beside the Allies after the armistice.
d5-7.st: The Italian military shrine at Mignano Monte Lungo is the resting place of 974 Italian soldiers. Most were men of the co-belligerent army that fought beside the Allies after the armistice. Their first battle was here, on Monte Lungo, on 8 December 1943: a failure with heavy losses, followed by success on 16 December. Today the terraced shrine looks out over Monte Lungo and the Mignano gap, and a small museum across the Via Casilina displays weapons and vehicles.

d5-8.ev: The US 36th Division fights for San Pietro while the villagers shelter in caves.

q.t: What does the museum use to tell the story of the battle?
o: Sound, darkness and John Huston's film footage
q.x: The museum in an old olive mill uses sound, darkness and John Huston's film footage.

d5-8.rem: San Pietro was left as it was destroyed in December 1943.
d5-8.st: In December 1943 the US 36th Division fought for San Pietro Infine, and the village was destroyed. It was left as it was after the fighting, which makes it one of the most powerful war sites in Italy. Its people sheltered in caves during the battle. A museum in an old olive mill uses sound, darkness and John Huston's film footage to tell the story of the soldiers and the villagers. Today visitors walk up through the roofless houses to the church and see the cave shelters.

d6-1.ev: Soldiers killed in the Sangro battles and the winter that follows are buried near the river.
d6-1.rem: 2,617 men lie here, and a memorial names more than 500 Indian servicemen cremated according to their faith.
d6-1.st: Sangro River War Cemetery is the largest Commonwealth cemetery on the Adriatic front. It holds 2,617 burials from the Sangro battles of November and December 1943 and the winter that followed. British, New Zealand, Indian and other soldiers lie here. The Sangro River Cremation Memorial names more than 500 Indian servicemen cremated according to their faith. Today the ridge the Germans held rises to the north-west, above the New Zealand and Indian headstones.

d6-2.ev: Canadians killed in the battles for the Moro, the Gully and Ortona are buried on high ground above the sea.
d6-2.rem: Of 1,615 graves here, 1,375 are Canadian, most from the December 1943 battles.
d6-2.st: Moro River Canadian War Cemetery is the heart of any Canadian visit to Italy. Of its 1,615 graves, 1,375 are Canadian, most from the December 1943 battles for the Moro, the Gully and Ortona. The cemetery stands on high ground between the river and the town, above the sea and close to where the fighting happened. Today the terraces of maple-leaf headstones look north to Ortona and south to the Moro valley.

d6-3.ev: Captain Paul Triquet and a handful of men hold the farmhouse against German counter-attacks.

q.t: Which regiment did Captain Paul Triquet belong to?
q.x: Captain Paul Triquet of the Royal 22e Régiment earned the Victoria Cross at Casa Berardi on 14 December 1943.

d6-3.rem: At Casa Berardi Captain Paul Triquet won the Victoria Cross, holding on with a handful of men.
d6-3.st: On 14 December 1943 Captain Paul Triquet of the Royal 22e Régiment reached this farmhouse and held on with a handful of men against German counter-attacks. He earned the Victoria Cross, and a memorial recalls the fight of the Van Doos. The open fields between the house and the Gully to the south-east are still there to see. Today Casa Berardi is a private house with holiday apartments, best viewed from the road.

d6-4.ev: Canadian troops fight house by house through the streets of Ortona over Christmas.

q.t: How long did the battle in Ortona's streets last?
q.x: Canada's most famous battle in Italy was fought in these streets for eight days at Christmas 1943.

d6-4.rem: Canada's most famous battle in Italy was fought in these streets for eight days at Christmas 1943.
d6-4.st: Canada's most famous battle in Italy was fought in the streets of Ortona for eight days at Christmas 1943. Walking from the southern edge of town along the Corso to the cathedral follows the Canadian advance. The battle cost the lives of soldiers and of 1,314 of the town's civilians, and the MUBA museum tells both stories, though it is closed for renovation. Today the Corso Vittorio Emanuele, the rebuilt cathedral of San Tommaso and the Aragonese castle above the sea trace the route.

d6-5.ev: The Seaforth Highlanders of Canada hold their Christmas dinner here, companies coming back from the line in turns.

q.t: Which regiment held its Christmas dinner in this church?
q.x: On 25 December 1943 the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada held their Christmas dinner here in the middle of the battle.

d6-5.rem: On Christmas Day 1943 the Seaforths ate their Christmas dinner here, a few hundred metres from the fighting.
d6-5.st: On 25 December 1943, in the middle of the battle for Ortona, the Seaforth Highlanders of Canada held their Christmas dinner in this damaged church. Companies came back from the line in turns while the fighting went on a few hundred metres away. The dinner became one of Canada's best-known war stories. Today the medieval church on Via Don Bosco keeps its 14th-century portal, though much of the rest was rebuilt after the war; it is usually seen from outside.

d7-1.ev: Men killed crossing the Garigliano and fighting for the hills beyond are buried near the river.
d7-1.rem: More than 2,000 Commonwealth soldiers lie a few hundred metres from the river they crossed.
d7-1.st: More than 2,000 Commonwealth soldiers lie in Minturno War Cemetery. Most were killed in the crossing of the Garigliano in January 1944 and in the fighting for the hills beyond. Their regimental badges include the London Scottish, Royal Scots Fusiliers, North Staffords, Hampshires and many more of X Corps. The ages on the headstones are worth reading. Today the cemetery is quiet and beautifully kept, only a few hundred metres from the river they crossed.

d7-2.ev: British troops cross the Garigliano, and engineers bridge the river under fire beside the ruined bridge.

q.t: Who blew up the 1832 iron suspension bridge?
q.x: The Germans blew up the 1832 iron suspension bridge in autumn 1943.

d7-2.rem: Here the Via Appia crosses the Garigliano, the western anchor of the Gustav Line.
d7-2.st: Here the Via Appia crosses the Garigliano, the western anchor of the Gustav Line. The Germans blew up the 1832 iron suspension bridge in the autumn of 1943, and in January 1944 British engineers bridged the river under fire. The width and current of the river show what the assault troops faced. Beside the crossing lie the Roman ruins of Minturnae, so ancient and modern war sit side by side. Today the bridge, restored in 1998, can be seen from the Via Appia.

d7-3.ev: The British 56th Division fights at the gates of Castelforte, a town the war almost wipes out.

q.t: Who finally took Castelforte in May 1944?
q.x: The British 56th Division fought at its gates in January 1944, and the French took it in May.

d7-3.rem: Castelforte was almost wiped out; its museum tells the Garigliano front from the civilians' point of view.
d7-3.st: Castelforte was almost wiped out in the fighting of 1944. The British 56th Division fought at its gates in January, and the French took the town in May. This small volunteer-run museum tells the story of the Garigliano front from the viewpoint of the civilians who lived through it, with weapons, equipment and photographs found locally. Today visits are by arrangement with the local association, and it is worth asking about the fighting for Monte Damiano and the civilian toll.

d7-4.ev: The French break through the Aurunci mountains, which the Germans thought too rugged for a major attack.

q.t: Why was the French attack here unexpected?
o: The Germans thought the mountains too rugged
The French had been ordered to Anzio
It came in deep winter snow
q.x: The Germans thought the Aurunci mountains too rugged for a major attack; the breakthrough unlocked the Gustav Line.

d7-4.rem: The French breakthrough in these mountains unlocked the whole Gustav Line.
d7-4.st: Between 13 and 16 May 1944 the French broke through in these mountains, which the Germans had thought too rugged for a major attack. The breakthrough unlocked the whole Gustav Line. In the days that followed, villages along this road, among them Ausonia and Esperia, also suffered the worst of the Marocchinate, mass rapes and killings of Italian civilians by some of the attacking troops. Today a roadside stop between Castelforte and Ausonia looks up at Monte Maio, the 940-metre summit to the north-east.

d7-5.ev: From this bluff the Germans watch the Texas Division try to cross the Rapido below.
d7-5.rem: Memorials to the 36th Division and a peace bell look down on the most painful American site of the campaign.
d7-5.st: On 20–22 January 1944 the US 36th Texas Division tried to cross the Gari, or Rapido, river below this bluff, while the Germans watched from here. After two nights the survivors were back where they had started, and the site became the most painful American place of the campaign. Memorials to the 36th Division and a peace bell stand on the edge of the village square, looking down on the crossing sites. Today the view takes in the river, the flat fields beyond and Monte Cassino dominating everything.

d7-6.ev: Soldiers of the French Expeditionary Corps, many from North Africa, are buried beneath headstones marked for their faith.
d7-6.rem: The largest French war cemetery in Italy holds soldiers of the French Expeditionary Corps, many of them North Africans.
d7-6.st: Venafro is the largest French war cemetery in Italy. It holds the graves of between about 3,400 and over 5,000 soldiers of the French Expeditionary Corps; sources differ, partly because graves from Naples were moved here in 1990–91. Many were Moroccans, Algerians and Tunisians, buried beneath headstones marked for their faith. The cemetery shows how many nations fought for Cassino. Today Christian crosses stand beside Muslim headstones, with the North African regiments named on them.
